¶
'''assertively''' (a̤-sėr′tiv-li), ''adv.'' In an assertive manner; affirmatively.

'''assertiveness''' (a̤-sėr′tiv-nes), ''n.'' The quality of being assertive, or self-assertive.
{{smaller block|As for this ''assertiveness'', one should admire it; it tends to the virtue of contentment.
{{right|''W. Shepherd'', Prairie Experiences, p. 114.}}}}

'''assertor''' (a̤-sėr′tor), ''n.'' [< L. ''assertor'', declarer, advocate, defender, < ''asserere'': see ''assert.''] See ''asserter''.

'''assertorial''' (as-ėr-tō′ri-al), ''a.'' [< LL. ''assertorius'' (see ''assertory'') + ''-al.''] Asserting a fact as true, but not holding it to be necessary. See ''assertory'', the common form.

'''assertorially''' (as-ėr-tō′ri-al-i), ''adv.'' In an assertorial manner; as an assertion.

'''assertoric, assertorical''' (as-ėr-tor′ik, -i-kal), ''a.'' [< ''assertor'' + ''-ic'', ''-ic-al.''] Asserting; assertory; assertive: as, an ''assertoric'' judgment. See ''assertory''.

'''assertory''' (a̤-sėr′tō̤-ri), ''a.'' [< LL. ''assertorius'', < L. ''assertor'': see ''assertor.''] Affirming; maintaining; declaratory; affirmative; assertive.
{{smaller block|We have not here to do with a promissory oath: . . . it is the ''assertory'' oath that is now under our hand.
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Cases of Conscience, ii. 5.}}
An ''Assertory'' Oath is made to a Man before God, and I must swear so, as man may know what I mean.
{{right|''Selden'', Table-Talk, p. 77.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Assertory proposition''', in ''logic'', a proposition stating something to be true, but not stating it as necessary.}}

'''assertress''' (a̤-sėr′tres), ''n.'' [< ''asserter'' + ''-ess.''] A female who asserts.

'''asserve†''' (a-sėrv′), ''v. t.'' [< L. ''asservire'', serve, aid, < ''ad'', to, + ''servire'', serve: see ''serve.''] To

help; serve; second. ''Bailey.''

'''asservile†''' (a-sėr′vil), ''v. t.'' [< ''as-''<sup>1</sup> + ''servile.''] To render servile or obsequious.
{{smaller block|[I] am weary of ''asserviling'' myself to every man’s charity.
{{right|''Bacon'', v. 240 (Ord MS.).}}}}

'''asses,''' ''n.'' Plural of ''as''<sup>4</sup> and of ''ass''<sup>1</sup>.

'''assess''' (a̤-ses′), ''v. t.'' [< late ME. ''assesse'', also ''accesse'' (whence by apheresis ''sess, cess''), < OF. ''assesser'', < ML. ''assessare'', fix a rate, impose a tax, freq. of L. ''assidere'', pp. ''assessus'', sit beside, be assessor to a judge, in ML. fix a rate, impose a tax, assess (cf. ''assessor''), < L. ''ad'', to, + ''sedere'', sit, = E. ''sit.'' Cf. ''assize.''] '''1.''' To set, fix, or charge a certain sum upon, by way of tax: as, to ''assess'' each individual in due proportion.
{{smaller block|His method of raising supplies was to order some rich courtier to pay a sum, and then sell this order to some speculator with the power of torturing the person ''assessed.''
{{right|''Brougham.''}}}}
'''2.''' To estimate the value or amount of (property or income) as a basis for taxation.—'''3.''' To set, fix, or determine: as, it is the province of a jury to ''assess'' damages.

'''assess†''' (a̤-ses′), ''n.'' [< ''assess, v.''] Assessment.

'''assessable''' (a̤-ses′a̤-bl), ''a.'' [< ''assess'' + ''-able.''] Capable of being assessed; liable to assessment.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|assert|346|asseveration}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''3.''' To state as true; affirm; asseverate; aver; declare.
{{smaller block|There is no proof of what is so commonly ''asserted'', that the heel is longer in proportion to the foot in Negroes.
{{right|''Huxley'', Anat. Vert., p. 419.}}}}

{{smaller|'''To assert one’s self''', to assume and defend one’s rights, claims, or authority; exert one’s influence; sometimes, to thrust one’s self forward unduly or obtrusively.}}
{{smaller block|The natural strength and firmness of his nature began to ''assert itself''. ''George Eliot'', Mill on the Floss, iii. 2.

While the struggle between the Emperor and the Pope absorbed the strength of both, it became possible for the people to ''assert themselves''.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', Prin. of Sociol., § 498.}}}}

{{smaller|='''Syn. 2.''' ''Assert, Defend, Maintain, Vindicate. Assert'' supports a cause or claim aggressively: its meaning is well brought out in the expression, ''assert yourself;'' that is, make your influence felt. To ''defend'' is primarily to drive back assaults. To ''maintain'' is to hold up to the full amount, defending from diminution: as, to ''maintain'' the ancient customs, liberties, rights. To ''vindicate'' is to rescue, as from diminution, dishonor, or censure: as, to “''vindicate'' the ways of God to man,” ''Pope'', Essay on Man, i. 16.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And as my vassals, to their utmost might,
Assist my person, and ''assert'' my right.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Pal. and Arc., l. 1,000.}}}}
{{smaller block|It is time now to draw homeward; and to think rather of ''defending'' myself, than assaulting others.
{{right|''Dryden'', Pref. to Mock Astrologer.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I will ''maintain''
My truth and honour firmly. ''Shak.'', Lear, v. 3.</poem>

If it should at any time so happen that these rights should be invaded, there is no remedy but a reliance on the courts to protect and ''vindicate'' them.
{{right|''D. Webster'', Convention to Revise the Const., 1821.}}}}
{{smaller block|'''3.''' ''Assert, Affirm, Declare, Aver, Asseverate'' (see ''declare''), allege, protest, avow, lay down. (See ''protest.'') ''Assert'' seems to expect doubt or contradiction of what one says. ''Affirm'' strengthens a statement by resting it upon one’s reputation for knowledge or veracity: as, “she [Rhoda] constantly ''affirmed'' that it was even so,” Acts xii. 15. ''Declare'' makes public, clear, or emphatic, especially against contradiction. ''Aver'' is positive and peremptory. ''Asseverate'' is positive and solemn.}}

{{smaller block|We can ''assert'' without assenting.
{{right|''J. H. Newman'', Gram. of Assent, p. 11.}}}}

{{smaller block|It is a pure impertinence to ''affirm'' with oracular assurance what might perhaps be admissible as a suggestion offered with the due diffidence of modest and genuine scholarship.
{{right|''Swinburne'', Shakespeare, p. 23.}}}}

<poem>Our Hebrew songs and harps, in Babylon
That pleased so well our victors’ ear, ''declare''
That rather Greece from us these arts derived.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Milton'', P. R., iv. 337.}}}}

<poem>Then all ''averred'' I had killed the bird
That brought the fog and mist.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Coleridge'', Ancient Mariner, ii.}}}}

{{smaller block|It is impossible to calculate the good that such a work would have done if half which is ''asseverated'' had only been proved.
{{right|''J. J. Blunt.''}}}}

'''assertable''' (a̤-sėr′ta̤-bl), ''a.''   [< ''assert'' + ''-able.'']   Capable of being asserted or maintained. Also ''assertible.''

'''assertation†''' (as-ėr-tā′sho̤n), ''n.''   [< ML. ''assertatio(n-)'', < ''assertare'', pp. ''assertatus'', assert: see ''assert.'']   An assertion.   ''Sir T. More.''

'''assertative''' (a̤-sėr′ta̤-tiv), ''a.''   [< ''assert'' + ''-ative.'']   Assertive.

'''asserter''' (a̤-sėr′tėr), ''n.'' '''1.''' One who asserts or maintains; a champion or vindicator.

{{smaller block|Harmodius and Aristogiton had assassinated Hipparchus from mere private revenge; but they were now called ''asserters'' of public liberty.
{{right|''J. Adams'', Works, IV. 488.}}}} '''2.''' One who asserts or declares; one who makes a positive declaration.

Also ''assertor.''

'''assertible,''' ''a.''   [< ''assert'' + ''-ible.'']   See ''assertable.''

'''assertion''' (a-sėr′shọn), ''n.''   [< L. ''assertio(n-)'', declaration, < ''asserere'', assert: see ''assert.'']   '''1†.''' The act of setting free; liberation.—'''2.''' The action of maintaining a cause or a claim: as, the ''assertion'' of one’s rights.—'''3.''' The act of stating something to be true.
{{smaller block|''Assertion'' unsupported by fact is nugatory. {{right|''Junius.''}}}}
'''4.''' A positive declaration or averment; an unsupported statement or affirmation: as, his ''assertion'' proved to be false.
{{smaller block|An ''assertion'' is as distinct from a conclusion as a word of command is from a persuasion or recommendation.
{{right|''J. H. Newman'', Gram. of Assent, p. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|The capacity of jelly [protoplasm] to guide forces, which Professor Huxley says is a fact of the profoundest significance to him, is not a fact at all, but merely an ''assertion.''
{{right|''Beale'', Protoplasm, p. 85.}}}}
{{smaller block|='''Syn. 2.''' Vindication, defense, maintenance.—'''3''' and '''4.''' Statement, asseveration, protestation.}}

'''assertional''' (a-sėr′shọn-al), ''a.''   [< ''assertion'' + ''-al.'']   Pertaining to or of the nature of an assertion; containing an assertion. [Rare.]

'''assertive''' (a-sėr′tiv), ''a.''   [< ML. *''assertivus'' (implied in adv. ''assertive''), < L. ''assertus'', pp. of ''asserere:'' see ''assert'' and ''-ive.'']   Positive; dogmatic; affirming confidently; peremptory; affirmative.
{{smaller block|Proposing them not in a confident and ''assertive'' form, but as probabilities and hypotheses. {{right|''Glanville.''}}}}

{{smaller block|An ''Assertory'' Oath is made to a Man before God, and I must swear so, as man may know what I mean.

{{smaller|'''Assertory proposition''', in ''logic'', a proposition stating something to be true, but not stating it as necessary.}}

'''asserve†''' (a-sėrv′), ''v. t.''   [< L. ''asservire'', serve, aid, < ''ad'', to, + ''servire'', serve: see ''serve.'']   To help; serve; second.   ''Bailey.''

{{smaller block|[I] am weary of ''asserviling'' myself to every man’s charity.

''assize.'']   '''1.''' To set, fix, or charge a certain sum upon, by way of tax: as, to ''assess'' each individual in due proportion.
{{smaller block|His method of raising supplies was to order some rich courtier to pay a sum, and then sell this order to some speculator with the power of torturing the person ''assessed.''
{{right|''Brougham.''}}}}
'''2.''' To estimate the value or amount of (property or income) as a basis for taxation.—'''3.''' To set, fix, or determine: as, it is the province of a jury to ''assess'' damages.

''Impost'', ''Rates'', etc. See ''tax''.}}

'''assessor''' (a-ses′ọr), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''assessour'', < ME. ''assessour'', < OF. ''assessour'', mod. F. ''assesseur'' = Pr. ''assessor'' = Sp. ''asesor'' = Pg. ''assessor'' = It. ''assessore'', < L. ''assessor'', an assistant judge, in ML. also an assessor of taxes, lit. one who sits by another, < ''assidere'', sit by: see ''assident'', ''assess''.]   '''1.''' One who sits by another; hence, one who shares another’s position, rank, or dignity; an associate in office.
{{smaller block|Don Quixote, . . . or his ''assessors'', the curate and the barber. {{right|''T. Warton'', Hist. of Eng. Poetry, I. 336.}}}}
'''2.''' An inferior officer of justice, who sits to assist a judge as a law authority; in Scotland, the legal adviser of a magistrate, with judicial powers.
{{smaller block|<poem>Minos the strict inquisitor appears,
And lives and crimes with his ''assessors'' hears.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Æneid, vi.}}}}
'''3.''' In England, a person chosen to assist the mayor and aldermen of a borough in matters concerning elections.—'''4.''' In some universities, as the Scotch, the title of the elected members of the university court or supreme governing body of the university.—'''5.''' One appointed to make assessments, especially for purposes of taxation.—{{smaller|'''Assessor of the vice-chancellor,''' in English universities, a deputy of the vice-chancellor appointed by him to hear causes and to be his vicegerent in court.—'''Nautical assessors.''' See ''nautical.''}}

'''assessorial''' (as-e-sō′ri-al), ''a.''   [< ''assessor'' + ''-ial.'']   Pertaining to an assessor, or to a court of assessors.

'''assessorship''' (a-ses′o̤r-ship), ''n.''   [< ''assessor'' + ''-ship.'']   The office of assessor.
{{smaller block|Be this as it may, his progress from the passive Auscultatorship towards any active ''Assessorship'' is evidently of the slowest. {{right|''Carlyle'', Sartor Resartus, p. 86.}}}}

'''asset''' (as′et), ''n.'' See ''assets.''

'''asseth†''', ''n.''   [ME., also ''aseth'', ''aseeth'', ''asethe'', ''assethe'', ''assetz'', etc. (= Sc. ''assyth''), < OF. ''asset'', ''aset'', ''asez'', ''assez'', in the phrase ''fere aset'', ''aset fere'' (< L. (''ad'') ''satis facere''), make amends, lit. do enough: see ''asset'', ''assets'', the same word, of later and different use in E.]   Satisfaction; amends.
{{smaller block|We may noghte be assoylede of the trespase bot if make ''assethe'' in that that we may.
{{right|''Religious Pieces'' (ed. Percy), p. 6.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Yit never shal make his richesse
''Asseth'' unto his greedynesse.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 5600.}}}}

'''assets''' (as′ets), ''n. pl.'', orig. ''sing.''   [< AF. ''assetz'', ''asetz'' (OF. ''assez'', ''asez'', ''asset'', ''aset'', mod. F. ''assez'' = Pr. ''assatz'' = OSp. ''asaz'' = Pg. ''assaz'', ''assas'' = It. ''assai''), enough, in the law phrase ''aver assetz'', have enough, taken into E. as ‘have assets’; < ML. ''ad satis'', lit. up to enough, equiv. to L. ''satis'', enough: see ''satisfy''.]   '''1.''' In ''law'': (''a'') Sufficient estate; property sufficient in the hands of an executor or heir to pay the debts or legacies of the testator or ancestor to satisfy claims against it. (''b'') Any goods or property or right of action properly available for the payment of a bankrupt’s or a deceased person’s obligations or debts: generally used to signify resources for the payment of debts, etc. {{smaller|Assets are ''real'' or ''personal''. ''Real assets'' are lands such as descend to the heir, subject to the fulfilment of the obligations of the ancestor; ''personal assets'' are the money or goods of the deceased or insolvent, or debts due to him, which come into the hands of the executor or administrator, or which he is to collect or convert into money.}}

'''2.''' Property in general; all that one owns, considered as applicable to the payment of his debts: as, his ''assets'' are much greater than his liabilities.—'''3.''' [As a singular, ''asset.''] Any portion of one’s property or effects so considered: as, these shares are a valuable ''asset.'' {{smaller|—'''Equitable assets.''' See ''equitable.''—'''Marshaling assets.''' See ''marshal'', ''v.''}}

'''assever†''' (a̤-sev′ėr), ''v. t.''   [< L. ''asseverare'', assert strongly, speak in earnest, < ''ad'', to, + ''severus'', earnest, serious, severe: see ''severe.'']   To asseverate.
{{smaller block|Anselmus . . . not only ''assevereth'' it, but also endeavoureth . . . to set out the true . . . proportion of it.
{{right|''Fotherby'', Atheomastix, p. 317.}}}}

'''asseverate''' (a̤-sev′ėr-āt), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''asseverated'', ppr. ''asseverating.''   [< L. ''asseveratus'', pp. of ''asseverare:'' see ''assever.'']   To affirm or aver positively, or with solemnity.
{{smaller block|<poem>Charity nigh chokes
Ere swallow what they both ''asseverate;''
Though down the gullet faith may feel it go.</poem>
{{right|''Browning'', Ring and Book, I. 85.}}}}
{{smaller block|='''Syn.''' ''Assert'', ''Affirm'', ''Declare'', etc. (see ''assert''); to say, allege, protest, insist, maintain.}}

'''asseveration''' (a̤-sev-e̤-rā′sho̤n), ''n.''   [< L. ''asseveratio(n-)'', an earnest declaration, < ''asseverare'', pp. ''asseveratus'', assever: see ''assever.'']   '''1.''' The act of asseverating; positive affirmation or assertion; solemn declaration.
{{smaller block|“My God!” cried the monk, with a warmth of ''asseveration'' which seemed not to belong to him.
{{right|''Sterne'', Sentimental Journey, p. 21.}}}}

'''2.''' That which is asseverated; an emphatic assertion.
{{smaller block|He [Leeds] denied with the most solemn ''asseverations'' that he had taken any money for himself.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., xxi.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
